lines.say: Four ancient traditions. Different holy books. And they all tell almost the same flood story. Coincidence?
First stop: ancient Mesopotamia. Over three thousand years ago, a poem called the Epic of Gilgamesh was pressed into clay tablets.
A god warns a man named Utnapishtim: build a giant boat, and save your family and the animals!
When the storm ends, he sends out birds. A dove, a swallow and a raven, looking for dry land.
Sound familiar? In the book of Genesis, Noah builds an ark for his family and the animals.
It rains for forty days and forty nights. Then Noah sends out a raven and a dove, and the dove comes back with an olive leaf!
The Quran tells it too. The prophet Nuh, peace be upon him, builds the ark, and it comes to rest on Mount Judi.
And in ancient Hindu texts, a man named Manu saves a tiny fish. The fish grows huge, and warns him: a great flood is coming!
Manu builds a boat, and the fish pulls it safely to a mountain. Later stories say the fish was Matsya, a form of the god Vishnu.
So why do so many traditions share this story? Scholars still discuss it, and every faith reads it in its own way.
Which version did you hear first? Tell me in the comments!
